title: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
summary: Proposition 41 adds a new article to the California Constitution requiring the State Auditor to conduct a public performance audit of any program that would receive money from a special tax before a citizen tax initiative reaches the ballot, plus a repeat audit every four years after any special tax created by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026 takes effect. It separately bars any new state tax enacted after January 1, 2026 from being excluded or exempted from the state's voter-approved spending limit (the Gann Limit), and says the state may not collect such a tax if it is exempted. It contains a poison-pill clause aimed squarely at Proposition 40, the same-ballot wealth tax: whichever of the two measures gets more yes votes nullifies the other.
what_it_really_means: The measure does two structurally different things under one title, and voters approving one are approving both. Sections 1 and 2 of the new Article XXIV create an audit regime that applies only to 'special taxes' — taxes whose revenue is legally restricted to a specific purpose, as opposed to general taxes that go into the General Fund for any use. Section 3 does something broader: it bars any new state tax, special or general, from being excluded from the Article XIII B spending limit (the Gann Limit) if enacted on or after January 1, 2026. The audits are the part supporters' ads foreground; the spending-limit lock is the part that actually determines whether a same-ballot tax measure can function as written.

The pre-election audit triggers early and runs on a clock outside anyone's control. Under Section 1(a), the State Auditor must begin auditing the programs that would receive a proposed special tax's money as soon as the initiative's backers certify to the Secretary of State that they've collected 25 percent of the required signatures — months before it is known whether the measure will even qualify for the ballot. The LAO's analysis confirms this: the audit work starts 'before it is known whether the initiative will qualify.' The audit must, at minimum, evaluate ten things listed in Section 1(b), from whether the program buys goods and services at the lowest cost, to how its costs compare with a private-sector analog, to explicit 'recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of at least 10 percent annually.' That last item is not neutral measurement; it directs the Auditor to go looking for a specific number.

If the initiative qualifies, the executive summary of that audit is printed in the official Voter Information Guide immediately after the Legislative Analyst's impartial analysis — meaning a program still awaiting a first dollar of new tax money gets a state-commissioned public report card, headlined with a savings target, sitting in the same pamphlet voters read right before they vote on whether to fund it. Section 2 repeats the process every four years, forever, for every special tax enacted by the Legislature or by voters after January 1, 2026, whether or not any controversy ever attached to it.

Both audit programs are nominally self-funding: Section 1(f) and Section 2(d) say the Auditor 'shall be reimbursed from the revenue generated by the special tax' once it's approved, as determined by the Controller. But the LAO's fiscal analysis is explicit that this only covers taxes that pass. For 'special taxes that do not ultimately appear on the ballot or are rejected by voters,' the one-time pre-election audit cost is paid from the state's General Fund — meaning taxpayers fund audits of tax proposals that voters never even got to decide on, or voted down.

The spending-limit provision in Section 3 is short, two sentences, and it is where this measure's teeth actually are. It says no state tax taking effect after January 1, 2026 can be exempted from the Gann Limit, and that the state 'shall not impose, collect, or enforce' any such tax if it is exempted. Section 4(b) defines 'exempted or excluded' two ways: either the tax's revenue sits in a special fund outside the General Fund whose spending isn't counted against the state's Article XIII B appropriations cap, or the Legislature has voted to raise the cap itself under Article XIII B Section 4. Proposition 40, on the same ballot, does exactly the first of these — its wealth-tax revenue is deposited outside the General Fund and is written to be excluded from the spending limit. That is not incidental; Proposition 41's own findings (Section 2, subsections h and i of the proposed law) describe 'special interests' repeatedly passing taxes 'exempted... from the state spending limit' and frame closing that path as urgent, without naming Proposition 40.

Section 5 makes the conflict explicit and mechanical rather than incidental. It states that any other initiative on the same ballot that either sets different audit rules for special taxes or contains a state tax exempted from the spending limit is 'deemed to be in conflict' with Proposition 41. If Proposition 41 gets more yes votes than that conflicting measure, Proposition 41 'shall prevail in their entirety, and all the provisions of the other measure shall be null and void' — even if the other measure also passed with a majority. The LAO's own analysis confirms the mechanism runs both ways: Proposition 40 contains a mirror-image poison pill naming Proposition 41. Whichever gets more affirmative votes wins outright; the loser's text is voided in full, not just the conflicting parts.

Section 9, labeled 'Legal Defense,' is not about audits or spending limits at all and would not be guessed from the ballot title. It provides that if the act is challenged in court and the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend it 'to the fullest extent possible,' the Attorney General must appoint independent outside counsel to defend it, and a continuous appropriation is made from the General Fund — 'without regard to fiscal years' — to pay for that counsel. This is a standing, open-ended claim on the General Fund to fund private litigation against the state's own elected law-enforcement officer if that officer's legal judgment differs from the initiative's drafters, structurally similar to provisions CalTax and allied groups have inserted in other recent initiatives to insulate their measures from a future Attorney General's discretion not to defend them.

The measure never mentions fees, assessments, or bond proceeds, and that omission matters more than it looks. Under Proposition 26 (2010) and existing case law, a regulatory fee or charge tied to a specific service or benefit is not a 'tax' at all under the California Constitution, and general obligation bond proceeds are borrowing, not 'proceeds of taxes' subject to the Article XIII B limit in the first place. Because Proposition 41 only restricts 'state tax' as that term already exists elsewhere in the Constitution, any revenue structured as a fee, charge, or bond continues to sit entirely outside both the audit requirement and the spending-limit lock, unaffected by this measure regardless of how large or how programmatically similar to a special tax it is.

fiscal_impact.state_cost: Increased State Auditor costs 'likely in the range of the low millions of dollars per year but would grow over time,' per the Legislative Analyst's Office, plus a few hundred thousand dollars per qualified initiative to print and mail the longer Voter Information Guide.
fiscal_impact.state_savings: Possible but unquantified. The LAO notes savings could occur only if policymakers choose to implement the State Auditor's recommendations and those recommendations prove effective; no savings are guaranteed or estimated.
fiscal_impact.local_cost: none identified by the Legislative Analyst's Office. The measure operates entirely on state special taxes and the state spending limit.
fiscal_impact.revenue_change: None directly. The measure creates no new tax and repeals none. Its indirect effect is on how future special-tax revenue can be structured: any new tax that would otherwise route around the Gann Limit could not do so, which could trigger the Article XIII B mechanism requiring excess state revenue above the limit to be refunded to taxpayers or spent on schools, reducing money available for the taxed program's stated purpose.
fiscal_impact.ongoing_vs_one_time: Mixed. The pre-election audit is one-time per initiative. The every-four-years audit is a permanent, recurring ongoing obligation for every special tax enacted after January 1, 2026, for as long as that tax exists.
fiscal_impact.narrative: The Legislative Analyst's Office is unusually blunt that it cannot size this measure: 'The net fiscal effect of Proposition 41 is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers.' That is not a dodge; it reflects that the measure's cost driver is the number and complexity of future special-tax initiatives, which cannot be predicted, and its savings driver is whether officials choose to act on audit recommendations, which is entirely discretionary. What the 'net effect unknown' framing leaves out is the asymmetry in who bears near-term cost versus who bears long-term consequence: the State Auditor's staffing and General Fund exposure for failed initiatives is a real, current-year budget item, while the spending-limit provision's effect on any specific future tax, including Proposition 40 on this same ballot, is binary and immediate if Proposition 41 outpolls it. The LAO flags that scenario directly under 'Potential Interactions With Other Propositions': if Proposition 41 gets more yes votes than Proposition 40, courts could find Proposition 40 conflicts with Proposition 41 and stop Proposition 40 from taking effect even though a majority of voters approved it.

tax_changes: Creates a permanent constitutional requirement that any new state tax taking effect after January 1, 2026 remain inside the Article XIII B state spending limit; the state may not impose, collect, or enforce such a tax if it is structured to be excluded from that limit.

Adds a one-time pre-election audit and a recurring four-year audit cycle as a precondition attached to special taxes proposed through the citizen initiative process or enacted after January 1, 2026 by the Legislature or by voters.

new_spending_areas: California State Auditor: new staffing and resources to conduct pre-election and recurring performance/financial audits of programs funded by special taxes
Secretary of State: additional Voter Information Guide pages to print and mail State Auditor executive summaries alongside qualified special-tax initiatives
spending.funding_source: Audits of special taxes that are approved by voters or the Legislature are paid from the revenue generated by that special tax, as determined by the Controller. Audits of special-tax initiatives that fail to qualify or are rejected by voters are paid from the state General Fund. The Section 9 legal-defense fund for the act itself is a continuous, uncapped appropriation from the General Fund.

control_and_power: The California State Auditor gains a large new mandatory audit docket and the authority to define, within the statutory list of ten required topics, how each audited program is scored, including a mandated recommendation for at least 10 percent annual budgetary savings. The Auditor must invite input from the Legislative Analyst's Office and, for ongoing audits, the public, but the statute gives the Auditor sole authority to write the findings and the executive summary that appears in the Voter Information Guide. Section 3 removes discretion from the Legislature and the electorate going forward: no future statute or initiative, however popular, can place new special-tax revenue outside the Gann Limit, foreclosing a tool the Legislature and initiative sponsors have used repeatedly since 1979 per the measure's own findings. Section 5's competing-measure clause hands unusual power to the relative vote share between same-ballot measures rather than to a simple majority threshold: a measure that earns 51 percent of the vote can still be nullified in its entirety if a conflicting measure gets a larger margin, even if both cleared 50 percent individually. Section 9 gives the Attorney General a duty, not a choice, to appoint and fund independent counsel to defend the act if the Attorney General's own legal judgment would otherwise lead the state not to defend it, funded by an uncapped, standing General Fund appropriation outside the normal budget process.
loopholes: The audit and spending-limit restrictions apply only to a 'state tax' as that term is already defined elsewhere in the California Constitution. Under Proposition 26 (2010), a regulatory fee, assessment, or charge tied to a specific service or benefit is legally distinct from a tax and is not covered by this measure at all; nor is general obligation bond revenue, which is borrowing rather than tax proceeds subject to the Article XIII B limit. A future revenue mechanism structured as a fee or bond rather than a special tax sidesteps both the audit requirement and the spending-limit lock entirely.

Section 3's spending-limit prohibition applies only to taxes that 'take effect on or after January 1, 2026.' Any existing special tax already excluded from the Gann Limit as of that date is grandfathered in and untouched by this measure, regardless of size.

The pre-election audit is triggered by 25 percent signature certification for a 'special tax initiative,' defined by whether the initiative 'contains a special tax.' A tax initiative could attempt to structure its revenue as a general, unrestricted tax deposited into the General Fund rather than a dedicated special tax to avoid triggering Section 1's audit requirement, at the cost of losing the political appeal of a dedicated-purpose tax and requiring only majority rather than two-thirds legislative approval if enacted by the Legislature.

Section 1(f) and Section 2(d) reimburse the Auditor 'from the revenue generated by the special tax' once approved, but set no cap on what the Auditor may spend preparing the audit beforehand, and the LAO states costs 'would depend on... the complexity of the programs being audited' without a statutory ceiling.

Section 5's conflicting-measure clause is written to compare vote totals between Proposition 41 and any measure that either sets 'different audit rules' or contains an exempted tax; it does not require the conflicting measure to be about a similar subject overall, so its reach could extend to future same-ballot measures well beyond tax policy if they happen to include any exempted-tax or audit-rule provision.

Section 9's independent-counsel provision is triggered when the Governor and Attorney General decline to defend the act 'to the fullest extent possible,' a standard the statute does not define, leaving contested what counts as sufficiently vigorous a defense and who decides the Attorney General fell short of it before independent counsel and General Fund spending are triggered.
unexpected_provisions: Section 9 ('Legal Defense') has nothing to do with audits or the spending limit. It compels the Attorney General to appoint outside independent counsel, funded by a continuous, uncapped General Fund appropriation 'without regard to fiscal years,' to defend the act in court if the Governor and Attorney General do not defend it to the drafters' satisfaction. This kind of self-defense clause is not disclosed anywhere in the ballot title or summary.

The measure's official title inside the text itself is the 'Improving Transparency, Effectiveness, and Efficiency in California Government Act of 2026,' a broader efficiency-and-accountability framing than the narrower ballot title voters will read, which mentions only audits and the spending limit.

Section 5 makes this measure and Proposition 40, the SEIU-UHW-sponsored wealth tax on the same ballot, mutually nullifying based on which gets more yes votes, even though nothing in Proposition 41's ballot title or summary mentions Proposition 40 or wealth taxes by name. The LAO's own analysis flags this as a 'Potential Interaction With Other Propositions' that could stop Proposition 40 from taking effect even if a majority of voters approve it.

Proposition 42, also on this ballot and also backed by Building a Better California, contains its own competing-measure clause aimed at the same wealth-tax subject matter; a voter approving Proposition 41 is also interacting with a second, related nullification fight over Proposition 42 without Proposition 41's title disclosing that connection.

The audit's required content list includes a directive that is a policy conclusion dressed as a measurement: Section 1(b)(10) requires 'recommendations on how the program could achieve a budgetary savings of at least 10 percent annually,' meaning the Auditor is instructed to produce a specific savings figure regardless of whether the audit's other findings support that program actually being over-funded.
pros: Supporters argue California's state budget has grown 79 percent since 2019 to more than $350 billion while outcomes in areas like homelessness haven't improved proportionally, and that voters deserve independent, public information about how a program is run before being asked to fund it further.

Robert Gutierrez, president of the California Taxpayers Association, argues the measure 'gives voters the chance to have a transparent, unbiased analysis of a proposed tax and the programs it would support... before they cast their vote,' with ongoing audits ensuring continued oversight afterward.

Denise LeDuc Froemming, president of the California Society of Certified Public Accountants, argues that 'independent performance audits give voters objective, credible information about public resources, strengthening accountability and public trust.'

Supporters frame the spending-limit provision as restoring the intent of the 1979 Gann Limit, which they say was meant to cap state spending growth and return excess revenue to taxpayers, arguing that repeated carve-outs for individual new taxes have hollowed out that check over time.
The measure does not raise any tax itself and imposes no direct cost on individual taxpayers; its stated aim is to make future tax proposals more transparent rather than more or less expensive.

Former California Controller Steve Westly argues that with Californians already paying some of the nation's highest state income and sales taxes, 'we need better transparency and accountability to make sure our tax dollars produce results.'
cons: SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, which sponsors the competing Proposition 40 wealth tax, argues Proposition 41 'isn't really about audits — it's a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax,' pointing to Section 5's mutual-nullification clause as the measure's real mechanism.

Opponents note that Proposition 41's largest funder by far is Google co-founder Sergey Brin, backing the measure through Building a Better California, and argue the measure exists specifically to defeat Proposition 40's exemption of wealth-tax revenue from the Gann Limit rather than to generally improve government transparency.

The League of Women Voters of California opposed the original 1979 Gann Limit as 'too inflexible to assure adequate government services in an uncertain future' and argues Proposition 41 extends that same rigidity to all future special-tax revenue, including voter-approved initiatives that generally cannot be amended by the Legislature without another vote of the people.

The League also warns the measure could require audits of programs, such as public campaign financing, that may not receive General Fund support at all, and that if the state is at or near its spending limit, Proposition 41 could prevent revenue voters approved for a specific purpose from actually being spent on that purpose.

Because the pre-election audit begins as soon as an initiative reports 25 percent signature collection, taxpayers can be on the hook through the General Fund for auditing a tax proposal that never reaches the ballot or that voters reject, a cost the Legislative Analyst's Office confirms is not covered by the tax's own revenue.

The measure's Section 5 nullification clause means a tax measure that wins a majority of the vote can still be voided in its entirety if Proposition 41 gets more yes votes, a result that departs from the ordinary rule that any ballot measure passing with a simple majority takes effect.

Section 1(b)(10)'s built-in instruction for the Auditor to recommend at least 10 percent in annual savings functions as a standing pressure campaign against every future special tax's home program, independent of whether that program is well or poorly run.

nonpartisan_analysis.summary: The LAO describes Proposition 41 as requiring one-time pre-election audits of programs that would receive special-tax initiative funding, triggered once an initiative reports 25 percent signature collection, plus recurring four-year audits of any program funded by a special tax enacted by the Legislature or voters after January 1, 2026. It also flags that the state 'might not be able to exclude new special tax spending from the [spending] limit' going forward. On fiscal effects, it estimates State Auditor costs in the low millions of dollars annually, growing over time, mostly reimbursed from the taxed program's own revenue once a tax is approved, but paid from the General Fund for initiatives that fail to qualify or are voted down; it also flags a few hundred thousand dollars in added Voter Information Guide printing costs per qualified initiative. Critically, the LAO calls the overall net fiscal effect 'unknown' and separately warns that if Proposition 41 outpolls Proposition 40 on the same ballot, courts could find the two measures in conflict and stop Proposition 40 from taking effect even if a majority of voters approved it.

Provides the measure's full constitutional text, campaign finance data, and background. It documents that the initiative was filed by Kurt R. Oneto on December 8, 2025, qualified for the ballot June 23, 2026 with about 979,000 valid signatures, and reports that Building a Better California, funded primarily by Sergey Brin along with other technology and business figures including John Doerr, Michael Moritz, Patrick Collison, and Eric Schmidt, is the dominant funder of the Yes on 41 campaign (through its June 30, 2026 reporting snapshot). It confirms Proposition 41 and Proposition 40 contain mirror-image competing-measure clauses that nullify one another based on relative vote share, and that Proposition 42, also backed by Building a Better California, contains a related nullification clause over the same wealth-tax subject matter. No committee had registered in formal opposition to Proposition 41 as of Ballotpedia's review, though SEIU-UHW campaigns against it through its Proposition 40 support committee.

Summarizes the measure as making it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring pre-election State Auditor review and by counting new special-tax revenue toward the state spending limit, which CalMatters notes could trigger automatic taxpayer refunds that reduce funding for other state programs. It identifies the core dispute as the same-ballot conflict with Proposition 40, quoting SEIU-UHW's argument that the measure is designed 'to trick voters into unknowingly blocking a wealth tax on billionaires' rather than to audit waste. Its campaign finance data, current to September 15, 2026, shows Building a Better California contributing $64.25 million to the Yes on 41 committee and no registered committee primarily formed to oppose Proposition 41 specifically.
